title: Emanuelle Goes To Dinosaur Land

jokes.text: I didn't realize we were still airing that. Cramer's been dead for six months.
jokes.setup: Someone on TV is asking if one of them is Jim Cramer, implying they're watching Mad Money
jokes.punchline: Jack casually reveals Cramer has been dead for six months, delivered as a throwaway correction
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of absurdist world-building delivered with perfect Jack deadpan. The joke works on multiple levels: it satirizes CNBC, it establishes Jack's casual relationship with power and media, and the economy is flawless — two sentences and a complete alternate universe. Justifies the 8+ because of character specificity and the confidence of the delivery implied.

jokes.text: The Astors, the Rockefellers, the Sbarros...
jokes.setup: Jack is listing New York royalty who will be at Cerie's wedding — Astors, Rockefellers...
jokes.punchline: ...the Sbarros. The mall pizza chain family is listed alongside genuine American aristocracy.
jokes.explanation: A textbook 30 Rock rule-of-three joke where the third item is a comedic grenade. The setup is perfectly straight, the list structure creates momentum, and 'Sbarros' is the ideal anti-climax — specific, recognizable, and hilariously beneath the previous entries. Jack's sincere delivery makes it land harder. Earns its 8+ for structure perfection and instant quotability.

jokes.text: You think I don't want to know what Pizzarina Sbarro is going to be wearing?
jokes.setup: Jack mentioned the Sbarros; Avery responds with the name of a Sbarro family member
jokes.punchline: Avery has already personalized the Sbarro family member with a ridiculous Italian-pizza-portmanteau name, revealing she's equally invested in this absurd social world
jokes.explanation: The name 'Pizzarina Sbarro' is a comedic gem — it immediately characterizes the absurdity of treating mall-pizza nobility as genuine gentry, and the name itself sounds exactly right. The callback deepens the joke and adds character dimension to Avery. High quotability because the name itself is the joke.

jokes.text: I'm on Dodecacil, the pill where you only get your period once a year. We're so close to beating that thing completely.
jokes.setup: Avery is explaining why she can't go to the wedding — she has a conflict she can't get out of
jokes.punchline: The conflict is her annual period; the drug name and the phrasing 'beating that thing completely' treat menstruation as a corporate enemy to be defeated
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurd pharmaceutical invention (a once-a-year period pill) and Avery's characterization as someone who treats bodily functions as obstacles to be optimized and eliminated — perfectly consistent with her type-A conservative warrior persona. 'We're so close to beating that thing completely' is a brilliant button that frames biology as a war campaign.

jokes.text: It's not really a spa. It's more of a fenced-in area in the Adirondacks.
jokes.setup: Avery says she's going to a spa for her period
jokes.punchline: She immediately self-corrects: it's 'a fenced-in area in the Adirondacks' — clinical, utilitarian, bleak
jokes.explanation: The understatement is deadpan and character-specific — Avery doesn't romanticize things. The correction from 'spa' to 'fenced-in area' does the work efficiently. Slightly below the top tier because it's a simpler joke structure.

jokes.text: 'Aloha' means hello and goodbye. So, aloha.
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery are parting; there's romantic/relational tension about what this goodbye means
jokes.punchline: Avery uses 'aloha' to simultaneously greet and dismiss, but framed as a linguistic observation — coolly ending the scene
jokes.explanation: A clever deployment of a familiar piece of trivia to do character work — Avery's poise in a charged moment is perfectly expressed through the word choice. Economy is near-perfect. The wordplay itself is not strikingly original but the use in context elevates it.

jokes.text: What's that supposed to mean, you dumb douche? Oh, it's starting. I should go.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'I'll see you in two weeks' as a loaded parting shot; Avery snaps back with a surprisingly coarse insult
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately recognizes the period-induced mood shift and uses it to escape the conversation
jokes.explanation: A tight two-beat joke: Avery's uncharacteristic vulgarity is the first laugh, then Jack's instantaneous clinical diagnosis ('Oh, it's starting') and self-preservation exit is the payoff. Works as a callback to the period pill setup.

jokes.text: I'm going to be in Spanx for 12 hours. My elastic line is going to get infected again.
jokes.setup: Jenna is complaining about attending three weddings in one day
jokes.punchline: The complaint escalates from a relatable grievance (Spanx) to a specific, grotesque recurring medical problem — 'infected again' implies this happens regularly
jokes.explanation: The 'again' is the key word — it implies Jenna has a chronic Spanx infection problem, which is both gross and perfectly in character for someone this narcissistic and self-destructive. Character integration is high because this couldn't come from anyone but Jenna.

jokes.text: If I have to sit through that alone, I will rent a car, set it on fire, and drive it off a waterfall.
jokes.setup: Liz says she doesn't care about having a date, then is asked about Floyd's wedding
jokes.punchline: The consequences of attending Floyd's wedding alone are described with escalating, baroque specificity — the three-step destruction plan is disproportionate and precise
jokes.explanation: The three-step escalation (rent → set on fire → drive off waterfall) is structured beautifully — each step raises the stakes and the specificity of 'off a waterfall' makes it absurdly precise. It's very Liz Lemon: dramatic self-pity rendered in vivid, irrational detail. High character integration.

jokes.text: I could set you up with my trainer. He's gay. But not when he's drunk.
jokes.setup: Jenna offers to set Liz up with her trainer; 'He's gay' seems like a dead end
jokes.punchline: 'But not when he's drunk' — a second subversion that reframes the whole thing as a disturbing possibility Jenna is genuinely offering
jokes.explanation: A double-subversion in three sentences: setup (trainer offer), apparent dead end (he's gay), unexpected reopening (not when he's drunk). The economy is exceptional — 11 words do enormous work. Jenna's blithe delivery of what is actually a troubling suggestion is perfect character comedy. High quotability.

jokes.text: Sexual time travel, just like my Cinemax softcore Emmanuelle Goes to Dinosaur Land.
jokes.setup: Liz describes going back through her 'gentleman Rolodex' to find a date
jokes.punchline: Jenna names a fake Cinemax softcore film — 'Emmanuelle Goes to Dinosaur Land' — which is also the episode title, making this meta
jokes.explanation: This is the episode title joke — meta-referential, absurd, and perfectly economical. 'Emmanuelle Goes to Dinosaur Land' is a brilliantly specific fake softcore title that also happens to describe the plot of the episode (revisiting old relationships = time travel; the show's absurdist DNA = dinosaur land). The meta layer is the icing. Earns its 8.5+ for originality, the meta dimension, and because Jenna delivering this as a casual reference is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Meet me in the handicapped stall in 10 seconds.
jokes.setup: Jenna is giving Liz romantic advice; the conversation seems to be wrapping up
jokes.punchline: Jenna abruptly solicits a sexual encounter with someone off-screen, delivered as a casual command — completely derailing the scene
jokes.explanation: A cold, abrupt exit line that perfectly capsulizes Jenna's character — mid-conversation she pivots to a casual tryst arrangement with the specificity of 'handicapped stall' (the least romantic possible venue). The '10 seconds' gives it a businesslike urgency that's funnier than if it were vague.

jokes.text: I saw this gorgeous woman putting glasses on her daughter's Mrs. Potato Head. The why is not important.
jokes.setup: Drew tells Liz he was thinking about her; she asks why
jokes.punchline: He saw someone putting glasses on a Mrs. Potato Head — the specificity is absurd, then immediately deflated by 'The why is not important'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Mrs. Potato Head with glasses' is a perfect absurd detail for why someone would think of Liz Lemon, gently insulting without being cruel. Then 'the why is not important' — dismissing the very question that makes the story interesting — is a beautifully confident move. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: What goes good with second chances? Oh, water. I'd like water.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Drew what she can get him to drink; Drew starts a romantic-sounding line
jokes.punchline: The poetic setup ('what goes with second chances?') deflates immediately into the most mundane request possible — water
jokes.explanation: A solid misdirection — the philosophical setup leads to the most anticlimactic beverage order. It also characterizes Drew as someone trying to be romantic but falling short, foreshadowing his overall dimness.

jokes.text: Oh, my hooks. I'm just so comfortable with them that I... [destroys painting]
jokes.setup: Liz and Drew are having a tender reconciliation moment; Drew is about to reveal something
jokes.punchline: The revelation is that he has metal hook hands, which he accidentally uses to destroy a painting — the comfort-with-disability punchline is delivered via property damage
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the hook hands is a masterful surprise — the cutaway structure (we don't know until the moment he destroys the painting) makes it a complete physical comedy bomb. 'I'm just so comfortable with them' as his explanation for the destruction is a perfect character tag. Earns 8+ for the structural surprise and the visual comedy payoff.

jokes.text: I was helicoptering into Zimbabwe, when I thought I saw somebody that I knew. So I waved from the helicopter, which, it turns out, is a big no-no. And the rotor took my right hand clean off.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Drew lost his hand
jokes.punchline: The explanation is preposterous: waving from a helicopter as the cause — presented with complete sincerity as if this is a reasonable thing that could happen to anyone
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Drew is established as devastatingly handsome but catastrophically stupid — the helicopter waving story is the perfect encapsulation because: (a) the cause is idiotic, (b) he genuinely doesn't realize it was his fault, (c) 'which, it turns out, is a big no-no' is peak oblivious understatement. High character integration because only Drew could tell this story straight.

jokes.text: And it turns out the person I was waving to was not my old football coach. Of course not. You were in Zimbabwe.
jokes.setup: Drew explains he was waving at someone he recognized in Zimbabwe
jokes.punchline: The person wasn't who he thought; Liz's sarcastic 'Of course not, you were in Zimbabwe' underlines the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Liz's straight-woman reaction grounds the absurdism and gets its own laugh. The Liz/Drew dynamic is perfectly illustrated — she's the only one who sees how insane this all is.

jokes.text: To celebrate my return from Africa, my cousin and I bought a bunch of fireworks. [loses other hand]
jokes.setup: Liz asks how he lost the OTHER hand after the Zimbabwe/helicopter story
jokes.punchline: The second hand was lost to fireworks — an even dumber, more preventable accident, doubling down on the theme of Drew's catastrophic stupidity
jokes.explanation: The escalation is perfect — the audience has already accepted one lost hand from a stupid accident, so the second lost hand from an even stupider accident is a beautiful comedic escalation. The structure mirrors the first story (dangerous situation + Drew's obliviousness) but with domestic fireworks making it even more embarrassing.

jokes.text: There's this strangler who's about to be executed, and I've got my hooks crossed.
jokes.setup: Drew explains he's in line for a hand transplant from an executed convict
jokes.punchline: 'I've got my hooks crossed' — a physical/idiomatic pun (fingers crossed → hooks crossed) delivered with Drew's trademark oblivious sincerity, about hoping a murderer dies
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. It operates on three simultaneous levels: (1) the wordplay pun 'hooks crossed' replacing 'fingers crossed' is physically precise and earned, (2) the dark irony of hoping for a murderer's execution, (3) Drew's complete lack of self-awareness about the morbidity. The economy is extraordinary — the entire joke is one clause. It became a 30 Rock quote that people remember. Comparable to the calibration examples provided: sharp, multi-layered, highly quotable, perfect character integration. Justifies 9+ across all dimensions.

jokes.text: Ow, it's hot. Yeah, of course it's hot. It's been in the oven. Now, who's the dumb one?
jokes.setup: After Liz rejects Drew, he grabs something hot from the oven and burns himself on his (apparently remaining) stump or oven mitt situation
jokes.punchline: Drew's triumphant 'Now who's the dumb one?' after burning himself proves he is, in fact, still the dumb one
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the Drew storyline — his attempt at a triumphant comeback immediately self-destructs because he burns himself, proving Liz's point beyond doubt. The irony is that he's trying to demonstrate intelligence and demonstrates the opposite in real time. 'Now who's the dumb one?' is an instantly quotable line because the answer is so obviously still him.

jokes.text: Feline Groovy? It's a pun. Because cats' paws have grooves.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces the movie he's doing — 'Feline Groovy'
jokes.punchline: He immediately explains the pun unprompted, as though the room might not get it — the joke is his over-explanation of an obvious pun, and the explanation is also wrong ('paws have grooves' is not how 'groovy' works)
jokes.explanation: The joke is Tracy explaining his own pun incorrectly — 'groovy' doesn't refer to paw grooves, but he thinks it does. This perfectly captures Tracy's confident, wrong relationship with knowledge. High character integration.

jokes.text: They're paying me exactly one million teachers' salaries.
jokes.setup: Tracy is excited about his Garfield movie deal
jokes.punchline: He quantifies his salary not in dollars but in 'teachers' salaries' — making both a flex and an inadvertent social commentary
jokes.explanation: Tracy's choice of unit — teachers' salaries instead of dollars — is inspired. It's simultaneously a brag, an accidental social critique of celebrity salaries vs. education, and a window into how Tracy's mind categorizes value. The phrase is instantly memorable and quotable. Earns 8+ for originality and the layered reading.

jokes.text: Go for the 'O' in your EGOT.
jokes.setup: Dot Com is encouraging Tracy to take a dramatic role
jokes.punchline: References Tracy's ongoing quest to win an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony — a recurring series joke about Tracy's absurd ambition
jokes.explanation: A functional running gag reference that rewards series viewers. Solid but not independently funny — its value is contextual.

jokes.text: Hard to Watch based on the book Stone Cold Bummer by Manipulate.
jokes.setup: Dot Com presents a serious dramatic script to Tracy
jokes.punchline: The title/author are pure absurdist comedy — 'Stone Cold Bummer by Manipulate' as a book title is maximally bleak and ridiculous
jokes.explanation: 'Stone Cold Bummer by Manipulate' is a perfect 30 Rock fake-title joke. 'Bummer' as a literary descriptor is bathetic, 'Stone Cold' makes it sound like a WWE event, and 'by Manipulate' as an author name is the perfect button — implying the book itself is emotionally manipulative by naming the author that. Economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: You say things like 'You don't know my pain,' and 'You watch your mouth, Tyrese,' and, in a less dramatic scene, 'I'll have hash browns.'
jokes.setup: Dot Com is pitching the dramatic film by quoting from the script
jokes.punchline: The escalating dramatic lines deflate with 'I'll have hash browns' — the mundane diner order amid intense drama
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in rule-of-three deflation — the first two lines establish Oscar-bait drama, and 'in a less dramatic scene, I'll have hash browns' is a perfect anticlimax. The qualifier 'in a less dramatic scene' is crucial; it implies the hash browns order is treated with the same weight as the other lines. Structure is near-perfect.

jokes.text: It's either this or I submit that animated film I drew about the Holocaust.
jokes.setup: Tracy is considering the serious film to win an Oscar
jokes.punchline: He reveals the backup plan: a self-drawn animated Holocaust film — the casual mention implies he's been working on this in his spare time
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The casual mention of a self-drawn animated Holocaust film as a Plan B for Oscar glory is pure absurdist character comedy — it tells us everything about Tracy's delusional relationship with prestige filmmaking. The 'I drew' specification implies a child-like crayon situation which makes it even better. Earns 8.5+ for originality, character integration, and the specificity of 'I drew.'

jokes.text: Nancy and Avery almost ran into each other at the elevator.
jokes.setup: Jack is juggling two relationships simultaneously at TGS
jokes.punchline: The near-miss at the elevator reveals the situation is becoming unmanageable — played as a horror beat
jokes.explanation: Functional plot comedy — the near-miss is funny contextually but there's no particular wit in the line itself. Works as a setup for the episode's escalating comedy of errors but doesn't stand alone.

jokes.text: I've prepared a very unromantic evening. First, we're going to see a documentary about female circumcision, and then we're going to eat too much Indian food.
jokes.setup: Jack needs to keep his date with Nancy asexual to avoid further complications
jokes.punchline: His strategy is to deploy maximum discomfort — a female circumcision documentary followed by excessive Indian food — as a romance prophylactic
jokes.explanation: Jack's strategic deployment of an anti-romantic evening is perfectly in character — he approaches romantic problems with the precision of a corporate strategist. The specific combination of documentary subject + gastrointestinal hazard is inspired. Character integration is high because this is exactly how Jack's mind would work.

jokes.text: Sometimes, the right thing and the hard thing are the same thing. I read that on a teabag.
jokes.setup: Liz delivers what sounds like a genuine piece of wisdom to Jack
jokes.punchline: She sourced it from a tea bag — deflating the philosophical moment into consumer packaging wisdom
jokes.explanation: A compact joke that works perfectly: the sincerity of the aphorism is immediately undercut by 'I read that on a teabag.' The beat of silence before the sourcing confession is what makes it land. Character integration is high — Liz both genuinely believes the wisdom AND reveals its humble origin without embarrassment.

jokes.text: You know what? Sometimes, I think... That's great. 'You know what? Sometimes, I think...' That's really annoying. I'm going to use that.
jokes.setup: Liz starts to give advice; Jack cuts her off and repeats the sentence fragment back to her admiringly
jokes.punchline: Jack announces he will steal her verbal tic as a manipulation tool — treating a normal speech pattern as a tactical asset
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of character work — Jack's predatory intelligence turns a nothing verbal tic into a tool to be harvested. It also perfectly characterizes the Jack/Liz dynamic: she provides the raw material, he exploits it. 'Okay, I hear it' when Liz tries again is a great button.

jokes.text: Okay, I hear it.
jokes.setup: After Jack tells Liz her 'You know what, sometimes I think...' is annoying, she immediately does it again
jokes.punchline: When Jack responds to her doing it again, she self-corrects with 'Okay, I hear it' — implying she only noticed it because Jack pointed it out
jokes.explanation: A tight callback button — three words that do a lot of work. The joke is that Liz is so oblivious to her own habits that she repeats the exact thing she was just called out for. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: I remember being born, of course. I remember learning how to ride a bike. But that was last year.
jokes.setup: Tracy is asked why he can't remember his traumatic childhood and lists things he DOES remember
jokes.punchline: 'But that was last year' — Tracy learned to ride a bike as an adult, delivered as a mundane clarification
jokes.explanation: A devastating piece of character-building comedy. Tracy claims to remember being born (absurd) and learning to ride a bike (relatable), then drops 'but that was last year' as a casual clarification — revealing he only learned recently while implying bike-riding and birth are equivalent memories. The delivery implied is completely deadpan. Earns 8.5+ for character integration and the specificity of the punchline.

jokes.text: I remember the summer my Webelos group went camping, and we were taken by the Hill People. Next thing I knew, summer was over and it was time for back to school shopping.
jokes.setup: Tracy is explaining what he does remember from his childhood
jokes.punchline: Being 'taken by the Hill People' is treated as a normal summer camp experience, casually bridged to back-to-school shopping — the trauma is completely unprocessed
jokes.explanation: Extraordinary absurdist comedy. 'Taken by the Hill People' is presented as a completely normal childhood experience (like going to camp), and the transition to 'back to school shopping' treats what is clearly a traumatic kidnapping as a pleasant summer interlude. The deadpan matter-of-factness is what makes it explosive. Tracy's psychological dissociation is both the joke and the character truth. Earns 8.5+ easily.

jokes.text: No, I don't. I was on a yacht with the Roots last week.
jokes.setup: Dot Com tells Tracy he needs to reconnect with his roots
jokes.punchline: Tracy takes 'roots' literally (The Roots, the hip-hop band) — a pun that reveals Tracy's literal-mindedness and proximity to celebrity
jokes.explanation: A perfectly executed malapropism-pun. 'Reconnect with your roots' is an obvious metaphor that Tracy takes literally as The Roots (the Jimmy Fallon house band/hip-hop group). The yacht detail confirms Tracy's lifestyle is exactly the opposite of reconnecting with his impoverished past. Economy is near-perfect — one sentence does everything.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz. Do you want to be a millionaire, hm? Mr. Dennis? No, no, no, Jose. Only babies out here. Don't you want to be a big boy? Ow!
jokes.setup: Liz arrives to find Dennis running a scam involving a child named Jose
jokes.punchline: Dennis is manipulating a child with condescending baby-talk ('Only babies out here. Don't you want to be a big boy?') followed by immediately hurting himself
jokes.explanation: Dennis's cringe-inducing manipulation of a child mentor is deeply in character — he's the worst possible adult role model treating a vulnerable kid as a prop for his grift. The immediate injury adds physical comedy. Character integration is high for Dennis.

jokes.text: Wait, are you planning to 'balloon boy' him? What was the one mistake those people in Denver made? One mistake? Yeah, there was no kid in the balloon.
jokes.setup: Liz notices Dennis has built something with a child and a balloon
jokes.punchline: Dennis is literally planning a 'Balloon Boy'-style hoax but his innovation is to actually put a kid in the balloon — presented as an improvement
jokes.explanation: Sharp topical comedy (balloon boy was a recent viral news event) repurposed to reveal Dennis's criminal ingenuity — his 'improvement' on the hoax is to actually endanger a child. 'One mistake?' as a response implies he's been studying the Balloon Boy case academically. Perfect Dennis character work.

jokes.text: This is a public park named after Ron Artest.
jokes.setup: Dennis calls his construction site 'a scientific facility'
jokes.punchline: Liz corrects him: it's a public park — named after Ron Artest, the NBA player famous for the 'Malice at the Palace' brawl
jokes.explanation: The Ron Artest name drop is the joke — the park named after the most violent player in NBA history is a pointed commentary on the neighborhood. Economy is tight. The joke rewards sports knowledge.

jokes.text: Yah, and like Jose, Ron dreamed of glory.
jokes.setup: Liz corrects Dennis by saying it's a park named after Ron Artest
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds by linking Jose's scam-balloon ambitions to Ron Artest's 'glory' — treating notoriety as inspiration
jokes.explanation: A solid button that characterizes Dennis's warped sense of aspiration — Ron Artest (brawler) as a role model for a child. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz. You'll be back! [as she leaves] Hey, what's going on, huh? What's your deal? Lesbian.
jokes.setup: Liz leaves Dennis's scam operation in disgust
jokes.punchline: Dennis calls after her, then when rebuffed by a stranger, immediately diagnoses them as a lesbian — his default explanation for any woman not interested in him
jokes.explanation: The snap pivot from yelling at Liz to propositioning a stranger to immediately diagnosing her rejection as lesbianism is pure Dennis — his ego protection mechanism is instant and absolute. The economy of just 'Lesbian.' as a complete sentence is perfect.

jokes.text: Way better than the Indian joint I go to in Boston. O'Doyle's.
jokes.setup: Nancy compliments the Indian restaurant they just ate at
jokes.punchline: The Indian restaurant she usually goes to in Boston is called O'Doyle's — an Irish-named Indian restaurant, suggesting the Boston Irish neighborhood's relationship with Indian cuisine
jokes.explanation: A brilliant one-name joke. 'O'Doyle's' as the name of an Indian restaurant in Boston does enormous character and world-building work — it implies the restaurant is run by or named after an Irish family, or is in such a Irish-Boston neighborhood that even the Indian place has an Irish name. Nancy's casual mention makes it perfect deadpan. Earns 8+ for economy and the implied world.

jokes.text: You know what I like after too much curry? A warm glass of milk and some John Philip Sousa marches.
jokes.setup: Jack and Nancy have just had a romantic dinner he was trying to keep asexual
jokes.punchline: His post-curry ritual is impossibly old-fashioned — warm milk and Sousa marches — positioning Jack as a Victorian-era patriarch trying to kill the mood
jokes.explanation: Jack's post-Indian-food ritual is perfectly absurd — warm milk is the most asexual thing imaginable, and Sousa marches (military parade music) caps it with an anachronistic specificity that is completely Jack Donaghy. The joke characterizes him as someone with genuinely bizarre patrician habits.

jokes.text: Come on, you sound like me at the Olympic Village.
jokes.setup: Liz says she's been through every guy and there's no one left
jokes.punchline: Jack compares her romantic exhaustion to his experience at the Olympic Village — implying he slept with so many Olympic athletes he ran out of options
jokes.explanation: A perfect throwaway Jack Donaghy boast — the Olympic Village reference implies he's had so many sexual partners among elite athletes that he exhausted the supply. It's characteristically Jack: the comparison is meant to be sympathetic but reveals extraordinary arrogance. Economy is perfect. Earns 8+ for character integration and effortless quotability.

jokes.text: Maybe I'll just lean into it and bring a cat in a baby stroller.
jokes.setup: Liz is resigning herself to attending Floyd's wedding alone
jokes.punchline: Her 'lean in' strategy is to embrace the eccentric-spinster archetype fully by bringing a cat in a baby stroller
jokes.explanation: A solid Liz Lemon self-deprecation joke — the specificity of 'baby stroller' (not a carrier, a stroller, implying full commitment to the bit) is the detail that elevates it. Good character integration.

jokes.text: He's told me his name, like, a million times, but I keep forgetting it. It's Wesley.
jokes.setup: Jack offers to introduce Liz to a wedding guest
jokes.punchline: Jack admits he's forgotten the man's name a million times — then remembers it: Wesley. The joke is that Jack thinks so little of Wesley that he can't retain his name despite repeated exposure.
jokes.explanation: A compact character joke about Jack's selective memory for people he deems unimportant. The pause before 'It's Wesley' implies genuine effort of recall. Functional.

jokes.text: Liz's immediate scream of 'No!' upon hearing Wesley's name / seeing him.
jokes.setup: Jack says Liz's date is named Wesley
jokes.punchline: Liz's visceral scream of horror — Wesley is her worst-possible-outcome date, a recurring nemesis
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat lands because of the setup (Jack's casual intro) and the implied history with Wesley. The physical comedy of Liz's horrified reaction is the joke — it needs no words. Works well in the episode's rhythm.

jokes.text: Of course I do. Excellent pantomime is supposed to look idiotic.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Wesley he looks idiotic doing pantomime
jokes.punchline: Wesley defends himself by insisting that looking idiotic is correct — the mark of excellence in pantomime
jokes.explanation: Wesley's defense of pantomime is perfectly delivered — the argument that looking idiotic is a sign of excellence is circular and absurd, but he makes it with complete conviction. A nice introduction to Wesley's insufferable-but-sincere character.

jokes.text: Liz, I'm going to guess that the last two months have been a lot of singles' events in gymnasia...
jokes.setup: Wesley returns; Liz has been on her romantic time-travel odyssey
jokes.punchline: Wesley guesses (correctly) the contours of Liz's dating misadventures with specific, posh condescension — 'gymnasia' (British plural of gymnasium) marks his character
jokes.explanation: Wesley's accurate mapping of Liz's romantic failures is both insulting and astute. The use of 'gymnasia' is a specific character detail — insufferably correct British plural.

jokes.text: The only thing wrong with me is that you hate me. So with that as my only defect, where do I rank with all the other men that you've been with?
jokes.setup: Liz expresses hatred of Wesley
jokes.punchline: Wesley reframes her hatred as his 'only defect' and positions himself as a competitive romantic option — the logic is both infuriating and technically sound
jokes.explanation: Wesley's argument is perversely logical — given everyone else's defects, being merely hated is a competitive advantage. The joke works because he's RIGHT, and Liz knows it, making it a cringe comedy moment as much as a character one. The structure is excellent: the rhetorical question at the end lets the audience sit with the uncomfortable answer.

jokes.text: Worms can do it with any other worm.
jokes.setup: Nancy and Jack have slept together; she says sex is a big deal
jokes.punchline: Jack's argument that sex isn't a big deal (since animals do it) gets extended to worms — the specificity of worms as the example, and 'any other worm,' is absurd
jokes.explanation: Jack deploying worm biology as a sexual philosophy argument is absurd but totally in character — he's arguing from a position of cold logic. 'Any other worm' captures the worm's complete non-discrimination, which is somehow funny as a sexual ideal Jack is implying.

jokes.text: Besides my ex-husband, you're the only other man I've slept with. Two men? That can't be true.
jokes.setup: Nancy reveals Jack is only her second sexual partner
jokes.punchline: Jack's incredulous 'Two men? That can't be true' — his shock is entirely a function of his own promiscuity, not a comment on her virtue
jokes.explanation: Jack's reaction tells us everything about his sexual history without stating it — 'that can't be true' is delivered as genuine bewilderment, implying his world has no frame of reference for monogamy or restraint. Perfect character integration.

jokes.text: After my divorce, I went out with my girlfriends, and I danced with a guy. Also, it was after midnight on a Saturday. So technically, it was a Sunday. A man had his hands on my hips on a day that was set aside for the Lord.
jokes.setup: Nancy says she has something bad to confess
jokes.punchline: The 'bad thing' is dancing with a man — but the escalating qualifications (after midnight, technically Sunday, the Lord's day) make her guilt proportional to a mortal sin while the act was completely innocent
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is a masterclass in escalation: each additional detail (after midnight → Saturday → technically Sunday → the Lord's day) ratchets up Nancy's guilt while making the actual act more mundane by comparison. The specificity of 'a man had his hands on my hips' treating hip-touching as transgression is both a character revelation and a culture joke. 'A day that was set aside for the Lord. There, I said it.' is a perfect button. Earns 9.0 for structure, character integration, and quotability.

jokes.text: Man, Catholic guilt. Am I right? Those nuns really messed me up. [Beat] Not me.
jokes.setup: Nancy confesses Catholic guilt about dancing; Jack commiserates
jokes.punchline: 'Those nuns really messed me up.' Then, beat, 'Not me.' — Jack starts to relate and then catches himself, correcting with a completely unconvincing denial
jokes.explanation: The timing and structure of this joke are near-perfect. Jack begins a relatable commiseration, almost commits ('Those nuns really messed me up'), then catches himself and delivers the denial with perfect Donaghy authority. The beat between the confession and the retraction IS the joke — it implies he absolutely was messed up by nuns, but will never admit it. Economy is extraordinary: the entire character depth comes from a two-word reversal. Earns 8.5+ for structure, economy, and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Because someone didn't come up here to scout the location first. Because someone else didn't sign off on the transportation budget. I never check that Earthlink account.
jokes.setup: Dot Com and Grizz realize they've taken Tracy to the wrong location (a copy shop that replaced his childhood building)
jokes.punchline: The mutual blame-shifting between Dot Com and Grizz — each assigning the screw-up to the other's failure — ends with the revelation that someone uses Earthlink (a dead 1990s ISP)
jokes.explanation: The Earthlink joke is the standout detail — using a defunct 1990s internet provider as a throwaway explanation for missing communication is a specific, dateable absurdity that lands as both a dig and a character note.

jokes.text: I slept on an old dog bed stuffed with wigs.
jokes.setup: Tracy's memories are flooding back as he sees his old neighborhood
jokes.punchline: The first memory is a dog bed stuffed with wigs — a specific, visual piece of childhood poverty rendered absurdly
jokes.explanation: The first memory in the cascade is the best. 'Dog bed stuffed with wigs' is a maximally specific piece of dark absurdism — it implies poverty (no real mattress), an inexplicable surplus of wigs (suggesting other household activities), and the image of a child sleeping on this is both terrible and hilarious. The specificity is what elevates it from generic poverty gag to 30 Rock-level absurdism. Earns 8.5+ for originality and image.

jokes.text: I watched a prostitute stab a clown.
jokes.setup: Tracy's childhood memory flood continues
jokes.punchline: A prostitute stabbing a clown — two archetypes colliding in a singular dark image
jokes.explanation: Six words, maximum impact. The combination of 'prostitute' and 'clown' is a deliberately absurd collision — both figures are slightly surreal, and the violence between them creates a nightmarish comedy image. Economy is perfect (10/10 — not a word wasted). The matter-of-fact delivery as a childhood memory is what makes it devastating.

jokes.text: Our basketball hoop was a ribcage. A ribcage!
jokes.setup: Tracy's memories continue to surface
jokes.punchline: The basketball hoop was a human ribcage — the repetition ('A ribcage!') implies Tracy is as shocked by this as the audience, having repressed the memory
jokes.explanation: Extraordinary dark absurdism. The basketball hoop as ribcage is a perfect comic image — poverty + neighborhood violence condensed into a single childhood object. The repeated 'A ribcage!' is a structural masterstroke: Tracy's rediscovering his own horror in real time, which doubles the comedy. Earns 9.0 for originality, structure, and the image's lasting power.

jokes.text: Some guy with dreads electrocuted my fish!
jokes.setup: Tracy's flood of repressed memories continues escalating
jokes.punchline: A dreadlocked man electrocuting a pet fish — the specificity of the descriptor and method creates maximum absurdity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'some guy with dreads' (not identified, just described) and the bizarre method (electrocuting a fish) is classic Tracy absurdism. Part of the escalating cascade that gets better with each memory.

jokes.text: I hate pain! I'm doing Garfield Three!
jokes.setup: Dot Com urges Tracy to use his pain for the Oscar film
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to all this excavated trauma is to reject it entirely in favor of Garfield Three
jokes.explanation: Tracy's rejection of emotional depth in favor of Garfield Three is a perfect character beat — after all that trauma, his response is to retreat into the lowest-stakes comedy possible. 'I hate pain!' as a philosophy is quotable.

jokes.text: And as soon as I make some copies of my passport, I'm never coming back here!
jokes.setup: Tracy is fleeing the neighborhood
jokes.punchline: The errand he needs to run before his dramatic exit is making copies of his passport — at a copy shop — a mundane administrative task that deflates the drama
jokes.explanation: The passion of 'I'm never coming back here!' is undercut by the practical errand (copying his passport at the very copy shop on his childhood corner). The mundane reason for being there in the first place deflates the dramatic return.

jokes.text: She put on red underwear. You would think it would clash with her hair. But it didn't.
jokes.setup: Liz demands to know what Jack was thinking when he slept with Nancy
jokes.punchline: Jack's explanation pivots from excuse to aesthetic observation — the color coordination note makes it both absurd and characteristically Jack
jokes.explanation: The fashion note ('you would think it would clash with her hair, but it didn't') as an explanation for a sexual decision is a brilliantly Jack move — he explains his own seduction in the language of a tastemaker making a considered aesthetic judgment. The 'but it didn't' is the perfect understated button.

jokes.text: Avery is cool, collected, descended from Swedish valley people. Nancy is a fiery, Irish nut job, descended from bog people.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why this is complicated with Nancy specifically versus Avery
jokes.punchline: The characterization of Nancy as 'bog people' vs. Avery's 'Swedish valley people' is Jack's genetic/ancestral explanation for personality differences
jokes.explanation: Jack's ancestral classifications ('bog people,' 'Swedish valley people') are a perfect expression of his anachronistic patrician worldview — he genuinely categorizes people by ethnic stock. The comparison is both offensive in character and hilarious because he's completely earnest. High character integration.

jokes.text: Floyd's wedding is at a Catholic church? Are they having a Mass? He converted for her. Meanwhile, when we were dating, and I wanted to check out that Unitarian church... Good talk, Lemon. Mm-hmm.
jokes.setup: Liz mentions Floyd converted to Catholicism for his fiancée
jokes.punchline: Jack is outraged that Floyd converted for Kaitlin (religious devotion as devotion) while when he was with Liz, even visiting a Unitarian church was too much — then immediately cuts off the revelation with 'Good talk, Lemon'
jokes.explanation: A masterful two-beat joke: Jack's indignation that Floyd converted (implying Jack wouldn't) reveals he couldn't even be bothered to visit a Unitarian church for Liz — making their non-relationship's failure suddenly concrete. Then 'Good talk, Lemon' is Jack shutting it down the moment he realizes he's revealed too much. The cut is the joke.

jokes.text: See how we help each other? I accompany you to Floyd's wedding. I hold your purse. This was meant to be. We're like Russ and Rebecca on Chums.
jokes.setup: Wesley is trying to convince Liz their pairing is destiny
jokes.punchline: His evidence of cosmic compatibility is that he held her purse and accompanied her to a wedding — plus a reference to a fictional British Friends knockoff called 'Chums'
jokes.explanation: The 'Chums' reference is the standout — a fictional British Friends (the show's name is itself a joke about British people calling friends 'chums'). Wesley's romantic logic (purse-holding = destiny) is perfectly insufferable. Character integration is solid.

jokes.text: I lost my job two days ago, and am now facing a little residency issue.
jokes.setup: Wesley is explaining why he needs Liz specifically
jokes.punchline: He reveals he lost his job and is facing visa/residency issues — the 'destiny' framing was actually a visa scam
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Wesley's romantic pursuit is immigration-motivated is a solid comedic turn — the 'meant to be' framing suddenly reads as calculated. 'A little residency issue' is classic understatement.

jokes.text: I can't suffer through the London Olympics. We're not prepared, Liz. Did you see the Beijing opening ceremonies? We don't have control over our people like that.
jokes.setup: Wesley explains why he doesn't want to go back to England
jokes.punchline: His fear of the London Olympics pivots to a comparison to Beijing's authoritarian ceremony precision — 'We don't have control over our people like that' treats Chinese political control as enviable
jokes.explanation: A sharp political joke delivered through Wesley's character: his admiration for Beijing's Olympic control is both a dig at Chinese authoritarianism (framed positively by an oblivious British man) and a self-deprecating British joke about democratic chaos. The layering is impressive and the specificity (2008 Beijing ceremonies) grounds it perfectly. Earns 8.0 for political layering and quotability.

jokes.text: Wesley sings a Chums theme song: '♪ I'll be here always / ♪ While the rains fall on whales'
jokes.setup: Wesley references Chums (the fake British sitcom) as a romantic metaphor
jokes.punchline: He actually sings what appears to be the Chums theme — 'while the rains fall on whales' is a sublimely nonsensical lyric that perfectly parodies maudlin British sitcom themes
jokes.explanation: The Chums theme song is a tiny comedic gem. 'While the rains fall on whales' is a masterpiece of fake-profound lyric writing — it sounds meaningful, uses British weather imagery, adds whales for inexplicable grandeur, and means absolutely nothing. The specificity of committing to an actual melody and lyric for a fake show is 30 Rock at its best. Earns 8.5+ for originality and the perfect fake-lyric craft.

jokes.text: Garfield effects test. Take one. And Act! Nermal, I hate you, Nermal! Almost as much as I hate Mondays! This is my lasagna! You hear me, Nermal? My lasagna!
jokes.setup: Tracy is doing a screen test for the Garfield movie in a motion capture suit
jokes.punchline: He delivers Garfield's lines with traumatized intensity — 'I hate Mondays' and 'This is my lasagna' become cries of genuine anguish from a damaged man
jokes.explanation: A spectacular collision of Tracy's childhood trauma with Garfield's famously banal catchphrases. 'This is my lasagna! You hear me, Nermal? My lasagna!' delivered with Method actor intensity is a perfect joke about Garfield as a character and Tracy as a person — his possession anxiety over lasagna maps perfectly onto a traumatic childhood of scarcity. The director's note ('maybe a little less intense... you're a cat who likes sleeping') adds a perfect straight-man beat. Earns 9.0 impact for being one of the funniest visual/performance moments in the episode.

jokes.text: A crack-head breastfeeding a rat.
jokes.setup: Tracy is explaining what he's seen that he needs to express artistically
jokes.punchline: The specific, horrific image of a crackhead breastfeeding a rat — the image is both dark and absurdly specific
jokes.explanation: Part of Tracy's artistic-trauma monologue, this is the most shocking image in the series — a crack-head breastfeeding a rat is maximally specific, horrible, and absurdist. The economy is excellent. Its place in the escalating list of horrors makes it land hard.

jokes.text: A homeless man cooking a Hot Pocket on the third rail of the G train. The G train, Nermal!
jokes.setup: Tracy's artistic testimony continues
jokes.punchline: The specificity of Hot Pocket (brand-name convenience food) + third rail (electrocution hazard) + G train (NYC's most maligned, least-connected subway line) is a multi-layered New York joke. 'The G train, Nermal!' addresses Nermal (Garfield's cat friend) as if he's still in character.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's top jokes. Three layers: (1) the image itself (homeless man + Hot Pocket + lethal cooking method) is brilliantly specific dark humor; (2) the G train is the perfect NYC detail — it's the subway line New Yorkers regard as a third-world transport; (3) 'The G train, Nermal!' shows Tracy has broken the wall between his trauma testimony and his Garfield audition, addressing his cat nemesis as his audience. The callback dimension adds extra craft value. Earns 9.0 across the board.

jokes.text: Feline Groovy can't tell my story, then I will win my Oscar elsewhere. Or I'll die trying.
jokes.setup: Tracy is building to a dramatic declaration about art vs. commerce
jokes.punchline: 'Or I'll die trying' — the escalation from Oscar ambition to potential death, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the Garfield scene — 'Or I'll die trying' is a cliché, but Tracy's complete sincerity sells it as character comedy. Below average for this episode.

jokes.text: Okay, so are you not doing this movie? Because that suit was made special! For your weird body!
jokes.setup: Tracy has stormed off the Garfield set
jokes.punchline: The director's concern about losing Tracy is entirely about the custom suit — 'For your weird body!' is an involuntary insult delivered in desperation
jokes.explanation: The director's breakdown reveals that his primary concern is the custom suit, not the actor — a perfect Hollywood commentary. 'For your weird body!' as an exasperated button is an unintentional insult that lands perfectly. Economy is sharp.

jokes.text: Excuse me, do you have a job? And are you here with someone?
jokes.setup: Liz spots a potential date at the wedding — a man named Mike
jokes.punchline: Her pickup criteria are entirely practical (employed? unattached?) with zero romantic affect — the most transactional possible approach to romantic interest
jokes.explanation: Liz's romantic desperation expressed through employment verification is a perfect character beat — she's moved past attraction to background checks. High character integration.

jokes.text: My name is Liz. I almost got 1200 on my S.A.T.s. And I need a date for this wedding. And I like your head shape.
jokes.setup: Liz is pitching herself as a date to Mike
jokes.punchline: Her credentials include almost getting 1200 (a mediocre SAT score), practical wedding need, and skull aesthetics — the least romantic three-point pitch imaginable
jokes.explanation: 'I almost got 1200 on my SATs' is the center of this joke — it's not a brag, it's a near-miss at a middling score presented as a credential. The escalation from academic non-achievement to 'I like your head shape' as a physical compliment is perfect. This is quintessential Liz Lemon: trying very hard and getting everything slightly wrong. Earns 8+ for character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Now may I tell you something? I'm a plushie. Is that a fraternity? Kind of. It means I belong to a group of like-minded people who dress up in mascot costumes. And have orgies in hotel rooms and state parks.
jokes.setup: Mike likes Liz's forwardness and wants to share something
jokes.punchline: He's a plushie — Liz asks if it's a fraternity, he says 'kind of,' then defines it with the mascot costume detail, followed by 'and have orgies in hotel rooms and state parks'
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured reveal. The misdirection (fraternity?) is set up, the quasi-acceptance ('kind of'), the costume detail seems mostly harmless, then 'and have orgies in hotel rooms and state parks' lands as a complete tonal reversal. The 'state parks' addition is the key detail — it implies outdoor public activities as well, which is somehow funnier than hotel rooms alone. Structure is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Our term for intercourse is 'yiffing'. Would you excuse me, please?
jokes.setup: Mike continues explaining plushie culture after Liz is clearly already fleeing
jokes.punchline: 'Yiffing' as the community term for sex — Liz's immediate 'Would you excuse me, please?' is the reaction
jokes.explanation: The button on the plushie joke — 'yiffing' is an actual furry/plushie community term, making it simultaneously accurate and absurd. Liz's immediate polite exit ('Would you excuse me, please?') is perfectly calibrated: not rude, just done.

jokes.text: Okay, fine. Let's get married. Oh, yeah.
jokes.setup: Liz is out of options; Wesley appears
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees to marry Wesley not with love but with the resigned acceptance of someone accepting a terrible job offer — 'Let's get married' as pragmatic concession
jokes.explanation: The reversal of romantic convention — marriage proposed in exhausted resignation — is perfectly executed. Wesley's 'Oh, yeah' reveals he's been angling for this all episode. The economy is perfect: four words for a proposal, two for the acceptance.

jokes.text: Nothing like being in church, having spent the night doing a bunch of bad crap. Am I right? Yes.
jokes.setup: Jack and Nancy are sitting in church during a wedding Mass, having just slept together
jokes.punchline: Jack's out-loud observation about the cognitive dissonance of church attendance after sinning — Nancy agreeing with 'Yes' confirms they're both aware of their situation
jokes.explanation: A functional situational comedy beat — the church-after-sinning observation is relatable and lands, but it's not particularly original. 'Am I right? Yes.' as a self-answered rhetorical question is a decent button.

jokes.text: You can't leave, Donovan. We're in the middle of Mass. You and I both know you have to stay until the final blessing.
jokes.setup: Nancy threatens to walk out of Mass upon Jack's confession
jokes.punchline: Jack deploys Catholic Mass protocol as a hostage negotiation tactic — correctly citing that leaving before the final blessing is prohibited
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character comedy. Jack weaponizes Catholic mass etiquette to prevent a breakup — using Nancy's own devout Catholicism against her. The joke is that Jack is correct on the theology AND is using it cynically as a stalling tactic. 'You and I both know you have to stay until the final blessing' treats religious obligation as a legal clause. Perfect Jack Donaghy move. Earns 8.5+ for character integration and originality.

jokes.text: Stall? [reading unscheduled Bible passages to keep Nancy in the church]
jokes.setup: Jack has trapped Nancy in the Mass; he needs more time and signals Liz
jokes.punchline: Jack wordlessly signals Liz, who understands and goes to the lectern to read additional Bible passages — the silent coordination and Liz's immediate comprehension is the joke
jokes.explanation: The visual of Liz immediately understanding Jack's one-word signal and going to the pulpit to read Bible verses is a beautiful piece of their friendship comedy. Their non-verbal shorthand and Liz's immediate willingness to conduct an unauthorized Mass reading is perfect.

jokes.text: 'But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he lay with his brother's wife, he spilled his semen on the ground.' Sorry. 'Then, Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin.'
jokes.setup: Liz is improvising a Bible reading to stall for Jack — opening the Bible at random
jokes.punchline: She lands on Onan (masturbation/coitus interruptus) and Zipporah (circumcision) — two of the Bible's most sexually explicit passages, read aloud in a wedding Mass
jokes.explanation: The joke is the Bible itself — Liz landing on two sexually explicit passages at a wedding Mass is both absurdist (the odds) and structurally perfect (escalating discomfort). 'Sorry.' after the semen verse is a perfectly mortified button. 'He spilled his semen on the ground' read at a wedding is a callback to the show's theme of Liz's romantic disasters. Earns 8.5 for the structure and the escalating passage choices.

jokes.text: Oh come on, Bible. Help a lady out.
jokes.setup: Liz has read the Onan and Zipporah passages and is desperately scanning for something appropriate
jokes.punchline: 'Oh come on, Bible. Help a lady out.' — addressing the Bible directly as if it's being uncooperative
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes — possibly the most quotable. 'Oh come on, Bible. Help a lady out.' treats scripture as an unhelpful service provider. The phrase 'help a lady out' transforms the Bible into an entity that owes Liz a favor. The economy is extraordinary: nine words that perfectly capture Liz's exasperated pragmatism and create an image of her alone at a pulpit negotiating with the Old Testament. Earns 9.5 quotability — this is a genuine TV quote. Earns 8.5+ craft for originality and perfect economy.

jokes.text: I seen a blind guy bite a police horse! A puppy committed suicide after he saw our bathroom!
jokes.setup: Tracy's repressed memory flood continues in an escalating monologue
jokes.punchline: A blind man biting a police horse; a suicidal puppy — each image is more absurd and dark than the last
jokes.explanation: 'A puppy committed suicide after he saw our bathroom' is a spectacular line — it implies the bathroom was so terrible it defeated a puppy's will to live. The escalation from 'blind guy biting horse' to 'suicidal puppy' maintains the show's dark absurdist momentum.

jokes.text: I once bit into a Merino and there was a child's shoe in it!
jokes.setup: Tracy's memory flood escalation continues
jokes.punchline: Biting into an unspecified food item and finding a child's shoe — the vagueness of 'Merino' (possibly a brand or food item) and the specificity of 'child's shoe' creates perfect absurdism
jokes.explanation: The 'Merino' ambiguity is actually part of the joke — we don't know if it's a brand, a dish, a pastry — but finding a child's shoe inside it is horrifying and hilarious regardless. The image of a small shoe in a food item is maximally weird.

jokes.text: I seen a hooker eat a tire!
jokes.setup: Escalation of memory flood
jokes.punchline: A sex worker consuming a rubber tire — physically impossible, absurdly specific
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-perfect: five words, maximal absurdism. The tire is such an impractical thing to eat that the image is completely committed. Part of a great escalating sequence.

jokes.text: A pack of wild dogs took over and successfully ran a Wendy's!
jokes.setup: Tracy's memory flood continues
jokes.punchline: Wild dogs running a Wendy's — 'successfully' is the crucial word, implying the dogs managed better than human employees
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the memory flood sequence and possibly the episode's top contender. 'Successfully ran a Wendy's' is the kind of punchline that could only exist in 30 Rock — the adverb 'successfully' does everything. The joke implies the dogs managed the franchise competently (taking orders, working the fryer, handling inventory) which is somehow more disturbing than if they'd simply destroyed it. The specific choice of Wendy's (not McDonald's, not Burger King — Wendy's, the most middle-tier fast food chain) is perfect. Rivals the hooks-crossed joke for best in episode. Earns 9.5 impact.

jokes.text: The sewer people stole my skateboard!
jokes.setup: Escalating memory flood
jokes.punchline: 'The sewer people' as a specific social group who stole his skateboard — implies an organized community of underground dwellers who have targeted him
jokes.explanation: 'The sewer people' as a defined community is a great worldbuilding detail — Tracy's neighborhood has an entire underground civilization with property crime capabilities. The theft of specifically a skateboard (childish, innocent item) from a child is a dark but funny beat.

jokes.text: The projects I lived in was named after Zachary Taylor, generally considered to be one of the worst presidents of all time!
jokes.setup: Tracy's memory flood continues
jokes.punchline: His housing projects were named after Zachary Taylor — one of the most obscure and worst-regarded presidents in history — which Tracy delivers as a civic grievance
jokes.explanation: A smart historical joke — Zachary Taylor is the perfect choice because he's both obscure and genuinely poorly regarded. That the housing project for some of America's most vulnerable citizens was named after one of its least distinguished leaders is a pointed social observation wrapped in absurdism. Tracy's outrage at the naming is character-specific.

jokes.text: I once saw a baby give another baby a tattoo. They were very drunk!
jokes.setup: Tracy's memory flood reaches its climax
jokes.punchline: Two drunk babies exchanging tattoos — the 'They were very drunk!' as an explanation is the button that makes the impossible image somehow worse
jokes.explanation: A perfect closing joke for the memory flood sequence. Two babies tattooing each other is already maximally absurd; 'They were very drunk!' as the explanation both deepens the image (drunk babies!) and implies this is Tracy's way of offering context/excuse. It's the most perfectly punctuated entry in the sequence. The exclamation mark in delivery caps the escalation. Earns 9.0 for being the ideal endpoint to one of the episode's best sequences.

tmdb_overview: Jack becomes even more entangled in his love triangle between Avery Jessup and Nancy Donovan, and he turns for advice to Liz, who is focusing on her own romantic problems. When Liz can't find a date to Floyd's wedding, she revisits her old boyfriends in hope that a spark will reignite. Meanwhile, Tracy continues his journey to earn his egot.
insight: Escalation-driven season finale hits 90.4 with 2.62 jokes per minute across 63 gags.
